content: Star anise, also known as star aniseed or Chinese star anise (Chinese: 八角, pinyin: bā jiǎo, meaning eight-horn), is a spice with a flavor profile similar to anise. It is derived from the star-shaped pericarp of Illicium verum, a small evergreen tree native to southwest China. The star-shaped fruits are harvested just before they ripen. This spice is extensively used in Chinese cuisine, Indian cuisine (as a key component of garam masala), and Indonesian cuisine. It is also a traditional ingredient in Chinese five-spice powder and is used to flavor the broth for the Vietnamese noodle soup phở. In the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, star anise is a common spice in the preparation of biryani. The flavor of star anise comes from anethole, the same compound responsible for the flavor of anise, despite the two plants being unrelated. In recent years, star anise has gained popularity in Western countries as a more affordable substitute for anise in baking and liquor production. It is notably used in the production of liquors such as Galliano, Sambuca, and pastis. Additionally, star anise has been used in traditional remedies, such as in teas to treat colic and rheumatism, and its seeds are sometimes chewed after meals to aid digestion. Star anise is also the primary industrial source of shikimic acid, a key precursor in the synthesis of the antiviral drug Tamiflu. While shikimic acid is produced by most autotrophic organisms, star anise has been a major source for its commercial extraction. Tamiflu is considered one of the most effective drugs for mitigating the severity of bird flu (H5N1), although some strains of the virus have developed resistance to it. In 2005, there was a temporary shortage of star anise due to its use in Tamiflu production. However, later that year, a method for synthesizing shikimic acid artificially was developed. Pharmaceutical company Roche now obtains some of its raw materials for Tamiflu by fermenting E. coli bacteria. As a result, star anise is no longer in short supply and remains widely available and relatively inexpensive. Star anise is cultivated in four provinces in China—Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Yunnan—and is harvested between March and May. The extraction of shikimic acid from the seeds involves a ten-stage manufacturing process that takes approximately one year. Reports indicate that 90% of the star anise harvest is used by Roche for Tamiflu production, though other reports suggest there is still an abundance of the spice in its primary growing regions. It is important to note that Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum), a similar-looking tree, is highly toxic and not suitable for consumption. Instead, it has traditionally been burned as incense in Japan. Cases of illness, including severe neurological effects such as seizures, have been reported after consuming tea made with star anise. These adverse effects are likely due to the accidental use of Japanese star anise, which contains anisatin, a compound that causes severe inflammation of the kidneys, urinary tract, and digestive organs.
